tldr: By having a Large Language Model (LLM) directly generate high-level policy code for humanoids and self-refine it using execution logs and video frames, this work achieves advanced loco-manipulation without task-specific reward engineering or human demonstrations.
hero_caption: Five simulation environments used for evaluation. They cover whole-body tasks that tightly couple locomotion and manipulation, such as ducking under low gates, passing through narrow gates, pushing a button, and pushing or lifting a box.
overview:
For humanoid robots to be useful in everyday life, loco-manipulation—coordinating whole-body walking and dexterous manipulation—is essential. However, traditional reinforcement learning requires painstaking reward engineering and retraining for every single task, while imitation learning demands costly teleoperation or video demonstration collection and retargeting.

To address this, the authors asked: why not freeze a pre-trained low-level whole-body policy (a foundation controller for walking and end-effector tracking) and let an LLM write the high-level policy code that runs on top of it? This is the core idea behind HuGo (Humanoid policy code Generation). Rather than calling a predefined skill library, the LLM constructs the control logic from scratch in code to compute target commands from observations.

Naturally, the LLM rarely writes flawless code on the first attempt. HuGo runs the policy in simulation or on hardware, letting the LLM analyze numerical trajectories alongside selected video frames. It diagnoses the causes of failure in natural language and runs a refinement loop that applies targeted code diffs.

In experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid across five challenging tasks, HuGo substantially outperformed a manually reward-engineered high-level RL baseline and approached the success rate of demonstration-based imitation learning. Furthermore, code generated in simulation transferred zero-shot to hardware, and the same refinement loop on real-world rollouts quickly closed the Sim-to-Real gap, boosting success rate from 20% to 90%.
contributions: Proposed HuGo, a hierarchical framework that directly generates executable closed-loop high-level policy code for humanoids from natural language task specifications, without task-specific demonstrations or reward engineering.
Developed an iterative self-refinement loop that combines numerical trajectories and selected key video frames to diagnose failure modes in natural language and apply targeted code diffs.

Demonstrated that HuGo substantially outperforms high-level RL across five simulation loco-manipulation tasks and across two different low-level policies, while also achieving zero-shot transfer and autonomous on-hardware refinement on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.

sections.heading: Why solve humanoid loco-manipulation with LLM code generation?
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation suffers from poor scalability because existing methods require task-specific reward design or human demonstration collection. This paper overcomes these bottlenecks by using an LLM to write high-level policy code on top of a frozen low-level controller and refining it through trial and error.
sections.details:
Recent humanoids can perform flashy acrobatic stunts like cartwheels and dances, but everyday utility demands more practical tasks: opening doors, pressing elevator buttons, and lifting boxes onto shelves. All of these require loco-manipulation, coordinating where to stand, where to reach, and when to move.

Yet acquiring these policies is notoriously difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) from scratch requires tedious reward engineering and days of retraining for each task. Imitation learning from human demonstrations faces heavy data collection burdens and the kinematics retargeting gap from human bodies to humanoids. Paying these costs for every new task is simply not scalable.

To overcome this, the authors adopted the "Code as Policies" paradigm, which has shown great success in manipulation. While having an LLM directly output humanoid joint torques is impractical, modern robotics already provides reliable low-level whole-body policies capable of tracking base velocity, end-effector positions, and torso height. The LLM can therefore focus on writing the high-level control logic that issues commands to this low-level policy.

This led to HuGo. HuGo does not rely on example code or predefined task skill libraries; it writes policy code from scratch using only observation definitions and the controller's interface specifications. Because the initial code is rarely perfect, an iterative refinement loop analyzes execution trajectory data and video frames, diagnoses issues, and patches the code incrementally. This loop works not only in simulation but also directly on real hardware (Unitree G1), dramatically lifting task success rates from 20% to 90%.

sections.heading: How does HuGo differ from existing LLM robotics and whole-body control?
sections.summary: Prior works primarily used LLMs to compose reward functions or glue predefined skills together, still requiring task-specific RL training or manual primitives. HuGo has the LLM generate and refine the closed-loop control code itself, evaluated step-by-step on a frozen whole-body controller without skill libraries.
sections.details:
### II-A LLM-Guided Optimization
Using LLM reasoning to optimize programs and parameters is an active research area. In robotics, methods like Eureka use LLMs to write reward functions, while others generate training curricula or multi-agent feedback. However, these methods still require heavy RL training after generating code, leaving the core training bottleneck unresolved. Other works use VLMs as video evaluators to verify task success. HuGo also uses an LLM as an optimizer, but it bypasses retraining entirely by directly editing the policy code based on rollout outcomes.

### II-B LLM-Generated Programmatic Robot Policies
Code as Policies pioneered using LLMs to write robot control code. Subsequent works used LLMs to write glue code connecting specialized modules like grasping and motion planning, or to generate behavior trees and skill graphs. However, these methods merely rearrange predefined skill libraries and primitives hand-crafted by humans. HuGo provides no primitive functions. Given only raw robot observations and input/output definitions for the low-level policy, it generates the complete closed-loop control logic—where to stand, when to reach, and how to transition states—evaluated at every time step.

### II-C Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Humanoid loco-manipulation typically adopts a hierarchical architecture with a low-level whole-body tracking policy and a high-level policy deciding what to do. Conventional high-level policies rely on residual RL, MPC-based demonstration collection, or pre-training from human videos. However, these require new rewards or new datasets for every single task. HuGo leaves the low-level policy completely frozen and generates the high-level policy directly from text descriptions as executable code.

sections.heading: How is the humanoid hierarchical control formulated?
sections.summary: The problem is framed as optimizing high-level policy code that sends step-by-step commands to a frozen low-level controller. Observations include robot poses, end-effector positions, and object geometries, while outputs consist of base velocities, target hand positions, and torso height.
sections.details:
This work formulates the humanoid loco-manipulation task $\mathcal{T}$ as a hierarchy between a high-level policy $\pi_{h}$ and a frozen low-level policy $\pi_{l}$. A task $\mathcal{T} = \langle \ell_{\mathrm{task}}, \mathcal{X}, \rho, S \rangle$ is defined by a natural language instruction $\ell_{\mathrm{task}}$, a state space $\mathcal{X}$, an initial state distribution $\rho$ (randomizing initial positions of the robot and objects), and a binary success evaluator $S$.

The high-level and low-level policies interact via the high-level command $a^h$. The low-level policy accepts commands in the following format:
- $a_{\mathrm{base}} \in \mathbb{R}^3$: planar base velocity (forward, lateral) and yaw rate (or target yaw)
- $p_{\mathrm{ee}}^{\mathrm{L}}, p_{\mathrm{ee}}^{\mathrm{R}} \in \mathbb{R}^3$: target Cartesian positions for the left and right end-effectors
- $z_{\mathrm{body}} \in \mathbb{R}$: target body height

At each time step $t$, the high-level policy $\pi_{h}$ receives observation $o_t$ and outputs $a_t^h$. The observation $o_t$ includes robot state $o_t^{\mathrm{robot}}$ (base pose, velocity, hand positions, height), task state $o_t^{\mathrm{task}}$ (poses of target objects and goals), and the previous command $a_{t-1}^h$. These are structured numerical vectors obtained from simulation or motion capture (MoCap), rather than raw images. The goal is to find a $\pi_{h}$ that maximizes task success across trials sampled from $\rho$.

sections.heading: From zero-shot code generation to multimodal refinement and Best-of-N
sections.summary: HuGo first generates closed-loop stateful policy code zero-shot. It then has the LLM write an analysis script over failed rollouts to extract numerical summaries and key frames, uses language feedback to apply targeted code diffs, and selects the best candidate via Best-of-N.
sections.details:
Querying an LLM API at the high frequencies (tens of Hz) needed for humanoid control is infeasible, but executing LLM-generated Python code runs easily in real time. The high-level policy $\pi_h$ is represented as executable code that maintains internal state $m_t$ across time steps (e.g., phases such as approaching, aligning, or pushing, alongside past command history).

### IV-A Zero-shot Policy Generation
The prompt $p$ contains only the task description $\ell_{\mathrm{task}}$, robot physical dimensions (such as pelvis-to-head offset and arm lengths) $\ell_{\mathrm{robot}}$, observation specifications $\ell_{\mathrm{obs}}$, and low-level command specifications $\ell_{\mathrm{act}}$. It contains no demonstration data, sample control code, or reference implementations. The LLM (gpt-5.4 in this work) consumes these specifications to output initial code $\pi_h^0$.

### IV-B Rollout Evaluation and Feedback
The initial code often fails because it cannot foresee all robot dynamics and contact behaviors. HuGo executes it from multiple initial states in simulation and collects failed rollout data $\mathcal{R} = (o_t, m_t, I_t)_{t=0}^T$ containing numerical trajectories and rendered image frames.

A key design is deciding what to show the LLM. Numbers alone often miss whole-body dynamics, like a robot tipping forward when extending its arms. However, full video cannot fit into the context window. HuGo prompts the LLM to write a dedicated Python analysis function $f_{\mathrm{analyze}}$ for the rollout. Running this function extracts a numerical summary $D$ (under 200 words) and key frame indices $k_{\mathrm{key}}$. Combining these with uniformly spaced frames yields a compact visual budget of $B=10$ images. From this summary and the images, the LLM generates diagnostic feedback $F$ explaining why the policy failed.

### IV-C Iterative Policy Code Refinement
Given feedback $F$, the LLM proposes a targeted code diff instead of rewriting the entire script from scratch. This preserves parts of the logic that already work well.
The refinement loop is structured into "Depths" and "Rounds". For each depth, it attempts up to 3 rounds of diff proposals. If an update improves validation success rate, the new code is accepted and advances to the next depth. If not, the failure history remains in context to guide another attempt. If 3 consecutive rounds fail to improve, the branch terminates as unrecoverable via local edits.

### IV-D Best-of-N Selection
Because LLM generation is stochastic, initial control strategies vary. Since local diffs cannot always overcome fundamentally flawed initial approaches, HuGo runs the entire pipeline independently $N$ times and selects the policy with the highest success rate via Best-of-$N$ selection.

sections.heading: Outperforming RL and acquiring complex skills for just $11
sections.summary: Across five whole-body tasks, HuGo substantially outperformed a meticulously reward-engineered RL baseline and approached demonstration-based methods. Video-based refinement was essential, and policies were obtained for approximately $11 and a few simulation hours per task.
sections.details:
### V-A Experiment Setup
Evaluations used the Unitree G1 humanoid in IsaacSim across the five tasks shown in Figure F2:
- **Low Gate Passing (LGP)**: Duck low to pass beneath two low horizontal gates.
- **Narrow Gate Passing (NGP)**: Turn sideways to squeeze through two narrow vertical posts.
- **Push Button (PBT)**: Walk up to a wall-mounted button and press it with an end-effector.
- **Push Box (PBX)**: Approach a box, push it to within 10 cm of a target, and hold it steady for 1 second.
- **Lift Box (LBX)**: Approach a box on a stand, grasp it from both sides with both arms, and lift it above 1.0 m.

Initial robot and object poses were randomized for every trial. To assess generality across controllers, experiments tested two low-level policies: an RL-based controller `rl_isaac` (50 Hz) and a state-of-the-art motion-prior controller `sonic` (10 Hz). HuGo was compared against a high-level RL baseline (PPO) trained for 384 million steps with dense manual rewards, and HDMI, an imitation learning method trained on human video demonstrations.

### V-B Main Results
HuGo dominated the RL baseline (Table I). Using `rl_isaac`, it achieved around 80% or higher success rates on 4 out of 5 tasks, reaching nearly 100% on LGP and NGP. In contrast, high-level RL failed to achieve high success on any task. In PBX, RL learned to push the box but failed to coordinate the staged sequence (approach -> align -> push -> hold steady), repeatedly overshooting the target. HuGo's generated code expressed this staged structure as an explicit state machine, completing the task reliably.

Compared to HDMI which relies on human demonstrations (Table II), HuGo matched its ~100% success on push-door passing (PDH) and achieved 81.25% on carry-and-place box (CPB) without any demonstrations (compared to HDMI's 98.4%).

### V-C & V-D Variation, Cost, and Reliability
A single generation run (Best-of-1) had high variance, averaging 43.9% success (std 23.4). Best-of-10 stabilized performance to an average of 79.1% (std 6.6). Most notably, generating and refining a single policy cost around $1.10 in API fees, meaning Best-of-10 cost only about $11. Parallel simulation completed the runs in a few hours, dramatically outpacing RL, which took over two days per task and required repeated reward tuning.

### V-E Ablation Studies
Ablation experiments confirmed the vital role of video feedback (Table III). Providing numerical trajectories as text only (Text Only) caused the average success rate to drop by over 40%. Numbers alone could not convey posture collapse prior to contact, proving images are indispensable. Furthermore, combining LLM-selected key frames with uniform frames achieved higher gains than using either frame selection method alone.

captions.F2: The five evaluation simulation tasks (LGP, NGP, PBT, PBX, LBX). Surrounding walls restrict navigation paths and randomized initial positions require the generated code to plan proper approaches and timing dynamically.

sections.heading: Zero-shot transfer and on-hardware self-refinement on the Unitree G1
sections.summary: Simulation-generated code transferred zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 with high success rates. When tracking lag reduced success to 20% on a hardware task, running the refinement loop using only real-world execution logs recovered success to 90%.
sections.details:
### VI-A & VI-B Hardware Setup and Zero-Shot Transfer
The real Unitree G1 humanoid ran the same `sonic` low-level controller in a MoCap tracking arena. Because observation and command interfaces matched simulation, the generated policy code ran without modification. Given lab space constraints, hardware evaluation focused on Push Button (PBT) and Lift Box (LBX).

Zero-shot transfer of top simulation policies (Table IV) achieved 93.3% success on PBT and 66.7% on LBX. As shown in Figure F5, the PBT code dynamically adjusted its approach vector when the button's position and orientation varied, correctly choosing whether to reach with the left or right hand. As illustrated in Figure F6, the robot successfully squeezed and lifted the box with both arms in LBX.

### VI-C Refinement on Hardware
However, not all code transfers seamlessly. Real-world friction and low-level tracking lag create Sim-to-Real gaps. One PBT policy that achieved 90% success in simulation dropped to 20% on the physical robot because the hand consistently stopped a few centimeters short of the button.

To address this, the authors deployed HuGo's refinement loop directly on the hardware. Failed real-world logs and camera frames were fed back to the LLM without human demonstrations or retraining.
Figure F8 illustrates this process. The LLM inspected the video and logs, diagnosing the root cause: the robot's base position and orientation were correct, but the end-effector was under-reaching. The LLM autonomously generated a code diff adding an `extra_press_margin` to push deeper. Consequently, hardware success climbed to 50% at Depth 1, 60% at Depth 2, and 90% at Depth 3, matching simulation performance.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: A new horizon for on-robot self-improvement
sections.summary: HuGo demonstrates that pairing frozen low-level controllers with LLM code generation enables complex humanoid loco-manipulation without reward design or demonstrations. While contact force maintenance and complex 3D geometric reasoning remain challenges, it establishes a powerful framework from simulation to real-world self-refinement.
sections.details:
HuGo provides an innovative framework where an LLM generates closed-loop high-level policy code on top of a frozen whole-body controller, autonomously debugging and refining it from rollout feedback. Across five simulation and two hardware tasks, it proved that high-precision loco-manipulation can be attained rapidly and inexpensively without reward engineering or expert demonstrations.

The authors also outline several limitations. A major bottleneck is the low-level controller's ability to maintain contact forces. When carrying a lifted box, the absence of force-holding control caused boxes to slip from the hands. Additionally, without explicit hints, the LLM struggled to deduce 3D geometric obstacle avoidance maneuvers on its own, such as swinging arms around a box to prevent collisions during the approach phase.

Promising future directions include building cross-task memory to accumulate refinement insights, distilling rollout trajectories into vision-based end-to-end policies, or using generated rollouts as seed data in RL replay buffers. HuGo's concept of robots debugging their own interpretable policy code opens an exciting direction for humanoid robotics.

takeaways: Freezing a low-level whole-body policy and having an LLM write stateful high-level policy code successfully bridges high-frequency control with high-level reasoning.
Combining numerical logs with key video frames allows the LLM to diagnose failure causes in natural language and self-correct via targeted code diffs.
Policies are produced for roughly $11 in API costs and a few simulation hours per task, eliminating manual reward tuning and lengthy RL training.
Simulation-generated code transfers zero-shot to hardware, and the same refinement loop can directly patch real-world execution failures to bridge the Sim-to-Real gap.
limitations: If the low-level controller cannot regulate and sustain contact forces (e.g., maintaining bilateral squeeze force on a box), high-level code cannot prevent physical slippage.
For complex 3D spatial reasoning, such as routing arms around obstacles, the LLM often fails to generate collision-free trajectories from feedback alone without geometric hints.
The framework assumes accurate numerical object and robot poses are available as observations, rather than operating end-to-end directly from raw camera images.
